questions.scenario: An insurer uses Claude to draft the payout recommendation that an adjuster reviews for each property-damage claim. The team wants to switch to a new prompt and a new retrieval configuration together as one release candidate. The offline eval set was built eight months ago, before a new policy wording was introduced, and compliance will not allow any customer-facing claim to be handled by an unvalidated configuration.
questions.stem: The team needs evidence that the candidate holds up on current, real claims before any adjuster or customer sees its output. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Route 10% of new claims to the candidate for two weeks, and roll back automatically if adjusters override more of its recommendations than the current version's.
Expand the offline eval set with synthetic claims that Claude generates from the new policy wording, then compare the two configurations on the enlarged set offline.
Run the candidate in shadow mode on live claims, logging and grading its output against production's while adjusters see only the current version.
Ask the most senior adjusters to try the candidate on a handful of recent claims of their choosing and approve it if they agree with its recommendations.

questions.explanation: Shadow mode runs the candidate on real, current traffic, so it exercises the new policy wording the stale eval set misses, but its output is only logged and graded, never shown. That satisfies the compliance rule that no claim is handled by an unvalidated configuration. Anthropic's agent-eval guidance notes that A/B tests and production monitoring measure real outcomes but let problems reach users; shadow mode gets the real-traffic signal without that exposure. Once the shadow results look good, a canary is the next step.

whyWrong.A: A canary exposes real claims to the unvalidated candidate, which compliance has ruled out. It is a later stage, after shadow results are in.
whyWrong.B: Synthetic claims help, but they reflect what Claude imagines claims look like, not the actual mix of current claims. The requirement is evidence on real claims.
whyWrong.D: A handful of hand-picked claims is a small, biased sample with no systematic grading. It cannot be repeated and does not show how the candidate performs across real traffic.

questions.mindset: When users must not be exposed but you need real-traffic evidence, shadow first, canary second.

questions.stem: A product team is running an online A/B test of two prompt versions for a help-center assistant. Before launch they agreed on a 14-day test sized to detect a 2-point change in self-service resolution rate. On day 3 the dashboard shows variant B ahead by 4 points, and the product manager wants to stop the test and ship B to everyone today. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Keep the test running to the planned size and duration, because stopping when an early lead appears inflates the chance of shipping a change that is really noise.
Stop the test and ship B, because a 4-point lead is double the effect size the test was designed to detect, so the result is already conclusive enough.
Stop the test and rerun both variants offline on the eval suite, then ship B if it also wins there, since offline results are more reliable than live ones.
Shift 90% of traffic to B for the remaining days so more users benefit sooner, while keeping 10% on A as a control group to confirm the result holds.

questions.explanation: The decision rule (sample size and duration) was fixed in advance precisely so that early swings would not drive the decision. Early in a test, differences bounce around, and repeatedly checking and stopping at the first good-looking moment makes false wins much more likely. Run to plan, then decide.

whyWrong.B: A large early gap is exactly what random variation often looks like on small samples. The planned size, not the size of the early lead, decides when the result is trustworthy.
whyWrong.C: The offline suite already passed before the online test. It cannot answer the online question (the real resolution rate), so it is not a substitute for finishing the test.
whyWrong.D: Changing the split mid-test alters the experiment and still bases the decision on an early, noisy read. It also does not provide the pre-planned evidence.

questions.mindset: Decide the stopping rule before you look, then honor it.

questions.stem: A fintech team runs its agent eval suite in CI on every prompt change. Six months ago it also began running online A/B tests on 5% of customers for major releases. An engineering director argues that the A/B tests now measure what actually matters (real customer outcomes), so the offline suite is redundant, and proposes removing it from CI to shorten release cycles. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Agree and remove the offline suite, since A/B results reflect real customer behaviour while offline scores are only a proxy that can drift away from reality over time.
Replace the A/B programme with the offline suite instead, since offline evals are faster and cheaper and the A/B tests expose paying customers to changes that have not been proven.
Keep the offline suite but run it only after an A/B test has been won, as a final regression check on the variant that is about to be rolled out to every customer.
Keep both: the offline suite gives fast, cheap feedback on every change before any customer sees it, and A/B tests are reserved for candidates that already pass it.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent-eval guidance treats automated evals, A/B tests, production monitoring and human review as complementary layers (the 'Swiss cheese' model): A/B tests measure real outcomes such as task completion, but they are slow (days or weeks to reach significance), need enough traffic, and put real customers in front of the candidate. Offline evals run in minutes on every change and catch regressions before anyone is affected. The efficient order is cheap and fast first, slow and real last: evals decide which candidates deserve an A/B test.

whyWrong.A: A/B tests are slow and reactive: without the suite, every regression, including small ones that would never justify a customer-facing experiment, reaches 5% of customers before it is noticed.
whyWrong.B: Offline evals cannot measure real customer outcomes such as task completion or retention. Dropping the A/B programme gives up the only ground-truth layer the team has.
whyWrong.C: That reverses the order. The cheap, fast check should gate which candidates consume slow, customer-exposing A/B capacity, not run after the expensive test has already been paid for.

questions.mindset: Evals, A/B tests and monitoring are layers, not substitutes: fast and cheap first, slow and real last.

questions.stem: A team compares a new prompt (B) against the current one (A) for a contract-summarization assistant on its 400-case offline suite, graded by a calibrated LLM judge. B beats A by 3 points overall. The suite is 80% short standard agreements and 20% long bespoke contracts; the bespoke contracts are where lawyers spend most of their review time and where the product earns its value. On the bespoke slice alone, B scores 9 points below A. What should the team do?

options.text: Ship B, because the agreed decision metric was overall suite accuracy and B won it; the bespoke slice is a small sample whose swing is more likely to be noise than signal.
Report results per slice as a standing practice, treat B's bespoke-contract regression as blocking, and diagnose those failures before revising B and re-running the comparison.
Ship B now and rebalance the suite to 50/50 so that future comparisons weight bespoke contracts more heavily, then revisit the decision when the next release is evaluated.
Ship B with an added instruction telling it to take extra care with long bespoke contracts, since the regression suggests it only needs a reminder on that category of document.

questions.explanation: An overall average can hide where a change helps and where it hurts. Eval design guidance says a suite should mirror the real task distribution, including the hard cases; when one slice carries most of the business value and risk, a regression there outweighs a gain on easy cases. Slice results should be reported routinely, and the failing bespoke transcripts read, so the team knows what B does wrong before it is revised and compared again.

whyWrong.A: Dismissing a 9-point drop on the highest-value slice as noise, without reading those failures, is a guess. Even if the slice is small, the right response is to examine the failing cases (and add bespoke cases if more confidence is needed). A decision rule that lets the highest-value slice regress unexamined is the wrong rule, not a reason to ship.
whyWrong.C: Rebalancing the set changes the yardstick after seeing the result, and it still ships a regression on the cases that matter most to users today.
whyWrong.D: A 'take extra care' instruction is a guess made without reading the failures. Until the team knows why B does worse on long contracts, it cannot tell whether a prompt reminder addresses the cause.

questions.mindset: Never judge an A/B result by the average alone; slice it by the cases that carry the value.

questions.stem: A team iterates weekly on a research-assistant prompt, scored by an LLM grader against a written rubric. This week's commit contained a prompt change and, in the same commit, a rubric rewrite the team felt better captured what a 'useful answer' means. The score rose from 71% to 79%, and the lead wants to report an 8-point improvement from the prompt change. What should the architect insist on before that number is reported?

options.text: Have a second, different LLM judge score the new outputs against the new rubric, and report the 8-point gain only if the two judges agree to within a couple of points.
Accept the figure, since the rubric rewrite was a deliberate improvement that brings the grader closer to what users value, so the new score is the more accurate one.
Re-score the previous prompt's outputs with the new rubric so both versions are judged by the same grader, and attribute only the remaining difference to the prompt change.
Re-run the new prompt five times under the new rubric and report the mean, since repeated trials show whether the 8-point gain is stable rather than a lucky run.

questions.explanation: Two things changed at once: the system under test and the instrument that measures it. A difference between a score produced by the old rubric and one produced by the new rubric says nothing on its own about the prompt. Re-grading the previous prompt's outputs under the new rubric (or re-running it, if outputs were not saved) gives a like-for-like comparison. Anthropic's agent-eval guidance stresses reading transcripts and grades to know whether a change in score came from the agent or from the eval; a grader edit is an eval change and needs the same one-variable-at-a-time discipline as a prompt change.

whyWrong.A: Judge agreement checks whether the grader is reliable, not whether the 8 points came from the prompt or from the rubric. Two judges can agree perfectly and the confound remains.
whyWrong.B: A better rubric may well be worth adopting, but adopting it moves the baseline. The jump mixes a real change in the system with a change in how the system is scored.
whyWrong.D: Repeated trials reduce noise, but all five runs are scored by the new rubric and compared with a baseline scored by the old one, so the confound is untouched.

questions.mindset: If you change the grader, re-grade the baseline; otherwise you are comparing two rulers, not two prompts.

questions.scenario: A software company is moving its internal code-review assistant, used by 1,200 engineers, from one Claude model to a newer one. The new configuration beat the current one on the offline eval suite, and shadow runs on a week of real pull requests showed no regressions. Leadership wants the change live quickly but does not want a bad release to reach every engineer at once.
questions.stem: Which rollout plan is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Release to a small share of engineers first, with rollback thresholds on agreed metrics set in advance, and widen in stages while the metrics hold.
Release to all engineers at once with close monitoring, since offline and shadow results are positive and a gradual rollout would only delay the benefit.
Keep running shadow mode for another month to gather more data, since only a longer shadow period can establish that the model is safe to release.
Let each engineer choose which model to use for a month, then adopt whichever one more engineers have selected by the end of the period.

questions.explanation: After offline and shadow validation, a canary or staged rollout is the standard next step: a small, reversible exposure that measures real outcomes, with the rollback criteria decided before launch so that the decision is not made under pressure. Widening in stages balances speed against the blast radius of a bad release.

whyWrong.B: A big-bang release is what leadership explicitly wants to avoid. Monitoring tells you something broke, but only after every engineer is affected.
whyWrong.C: Shadow mode cannot measure how users respond to or act on the output. More shadow time delays the release without answering the remaining question.
whyWrong.D: Self-selection makes the groups non-comparable, and popularity is not the agreed success metric. It also gives up control of the rollout.

questions.mindset: Offline, then shadow, then canary with pre-set rollback triggers: widen exposure only as evidence accumulates.

questions.stem: For two months, a team has fixed its HR policy assistant one complaint at a time: each week someone adds a sentence to the system prompt addressing that week's worst complaint. The prompt has grown to 4,000 words, and the eval score is flat. The architect wants the next month of work to produce measurable improvement. What should they do FIRST?

options.text: Move to a larger model, since a prompt that has grown this long without any improvement is a sign that the current model cannot follow so many instructions at once.
Ask Claude to rewrite the 4,000-word prompt into a shorter, cleaner version and ship it as long as the eval score does not drop when it is run on the suite.
Add each week's complaint as an extra few-shot example rather than a new rule, since examples steer Claude's behaviour more reliably than written instructions.
Review a sample of failing eval cases, group the failures into root-cause categories, and target the largest category with one change at a time.

questions.explanation: Patching individual complaints is reactive and gives no sense of which problems are common. Reading a sample of failing transcripts, labelling each failure's root cause and counting the categories shows where the biggest gains are. Anthropic's agent-eval guidance notes that manual transcript review is how teams build intuition for failure modes. Fixing the largest category with one controlled change, and measuring it against the eval, turns iteration into a disciplined loop.

whyWrong.A: Nothing shows the model is the bottleneck. A larger model costs more and may not fix whatever the failures actually have in common.
whyWrong.B: Tidying the prompt may be worthwhile later, but it does not identify what is failing. Holding the score flat is not improvement.
whyWrong.C: Swapping rules for examples keeps the same one-complaint-at-a-time approach. Without knowing which failures dominate, the team is still guessing.

questions.mindset: Count your failures by cause before you fix any of them.

questions.stem: A team tests a new prompt for an invoice-question assistant. The automated eval reports variant B down 8 points versus A on numeric answers. Before reverting, the architect reads 30 of B's failed transcripts and finds that most answers are correct but written as '$1,200.00' where the expected answer is '1200', and that a few test cases have expected answers that contradict the source invoice. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate next? Choose TWO.

options.text: Revert to variant A immediately, since an 8-point drop on the official eval is a clear regression regardless of what the transcripts show.
Fix the grader so it normalizes numeric formats before comparing, then rerun both variants on the same suite to get a fair comparison.
Add an instruction to variant B to always output bare numbers, so its answers match the expected format and the score recovers.
Switch the numeric grader to an LLM judge, because a model will recognize equivalent formats better than any code-based comparison.
Correct or remove the test cases whose expected answers conflict with the source invoices, recording the change so future comparisons use the fixed set.

questions.explanation: The transcripts show the drop is mostly an eval bug, not a model regression: the grader is too strict about format, and some reference answers are wrong. Fix the grader (normalize numbers, which a code grader can do deterministically), repair the bad test cases, then rerun both variants on the corrected suite. Anthropic's guidance stresses reading transcripts precisely because graders and tasks can be broken.

whyWrong.A: Reverting trusts a score that the transcripts have shown to be wrong. The decision should wait for a corrected eval.
whyWrong.C: Changing the product's output to satisfy a broken grader hides the grader bug, and users may prefer the formatted amounts.
whyWrong.D: An LLM judge adds cost and variability for a problem that deterministic normalization solves exactly. Use code where code can do the job.

questions.mindset: Before trusting a score change, read the transcripts; a broken grader or test case can fake a regression.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company runs a two-week online A/B test of a friendlier, more accommodating prompt for its returns assistant. The pre-agreed primary metric is customer satisfaction (CSAT); the pre-agreed guardrails are the rate of refunds approved outside policy and the repeat-contact rate. At the end, variant B lifts CSAT by 6 points, but out-of-policy refunds rise from 0.4% to 1.9%; repeat contacts are unchanged.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions are the BEST response to these results? Choose TWO.

options.text: Do not ship B as tested, because it breached a pre-agreed guardrail metric, even though it clearly won on the primary metric.
Ship B, because CSAT was the primary metric and the extra refunds are small enough to treat as an acceptable cost of happier customers.
Ship B to half of customers permanently, so the company keeps some of the CSAT gain while limiting the extra refund cost.
Investigate the out-of-policy refunds in B's transcripts, revise the variant to keep its tone while enforcing policy, and test the revision again.
Drop the refund guardrail from future tests of this assistant, since it conflicts with the primary goal of improving customer satisfaction.

questions.explanation: Guardrail metrics exist so that a win on the primary metric cannot hide damage elsewhere. B breached one, so it fails the decision rule agreed before the test. The productive next step is to find out why (for example, the accommodating tone may be leaking into refund decisions), fix that while keeping what drove CSAT, and run another test.

whyWrong.B: Overriding a pre-agreed guardrail after seeing the results defeats the point of setting it, and a nearly fivefold rise in out-of-policy refunds is a real financial and governance problem.
whyWrong.C: Splitting traffic permanently still ships a variant that breaks policy to half the customers. It is a compromise that ignores the breach rather than fixing it.
whyWrong.E: Removing the guardrail because a variant failed it is moving the goalposts. The policy risk does not go away because it is no longer measured.

questions.mindset: A primary-metric win that breaks a guardrail is a failed test: diagnose, revise, re-test.

questions.scenario: A university's IT help assistant answers staff questions from a knowledge base using retrieval. About 15% of answers on the eval set are wrong. One engineer is sure the retriever is the problem and wants to replace the vector store; another is sure the prompt is the problem and wants to rewrite it. Today the system logs only the question and the final answer.
questions.stem: What should the architect do FIRST to settle where the failures come from?

options.text: Rewrite the prompt to tell Claude to rely only on the knowledge base, since that change is cheaper than replacing the vector store and quick to test.
Log the retrieved passages with each answer and check, for each failing case, whether the passage that contains the correct answer was retrieved.
Replace the vector store with a hybrid keyword-and-embedding search, since hybrid retrieval generally performs better than pure embedding search.
Run the failing questions on a larger model with the same pipeline, since a stronger model will show whether the remaining errors are reasoning failures.

questions.explanation: A RAG failure is either a retrieval failure (the right passage never reached Claude) or a generation failure (it did, and the answer was still wrong). Logging retrieved context and checking whether it contains the answer splits the 15% into those two buckets, so each engineer's fix can be applied where the data says it belongs.

whyWrong.A: If the right passage was never retrieved, no prompt change can produce the right answer. This picks a fix before diagnosing.
whyWrong.C: Hybrid search can help retrieval, but it is a significant change made on a guess. If most failures are generation-side, it would not help.
whyWrong.D: A larger model cannot answer correctly from context that lacks the answer. This also changes a third variable without first separating the two suspected layers.

questions.mindset: In RAG, first ask whether the answer was in the context; that one check splits retrieval failures from generation failures.

questions.stem: A scheduling agent books meeting rooms through a `create_booking` tool whose schema has a `start_time` string parameter described only as 'when the meeting starts'. About one call in five fails, and the backend returns a generic 'invalid request' error. Traces show the agent passing values such as 'next Tuesday 3pm' and '15:00', while the backend expects an ISO 8601 timestamp with a time zone. The agent often gives up after the error. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Switch the agent to a larger model, since a more capable model is better at inferring which format an API expects from the parameter's name and context.
Add a sentence to the system prompt reminding the agent to be careful with dates and times and to double-check its tool arguments before every call it makes.
State the required format with an example in the parameter description, and make the tool return an error that says what was wrong and how to fix it.
Add a retry loop that resends the failed call unchanged up to three times, since many tool errors are transient and succeed on a second attempt.

questions.explanation: This is a tool-design failure, not a model or reasoning failure. The tool definition never states the format, and the error message gives the agent nothing to correct. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends unambiguous parameter descriptions and error responses that explain how to fix the call, so the agent can recover on its own.

whyWrong.A: The format is not stated anywhere for any model to read. A bigger model guesses better, at higher cost, but the definition is still ambiguous.
whyWrong.B: A vague 'be careful' instruction does not tell the agent what format is required. The fix belongs in the tool definition, where the parameter is defined.
whyWrong.D: The error is not transient: resending the same malformed value fails every time. Retries only add latency and cost.

questions.mindset: When the model misuses a tool, fix the tool's description and error messages before blaming the model.

questions.stem: A support team's ticket-priority prompt includes three worked examples, all of them password-reset tickets labelled 'Low'. Since the examples were added, the eval shows the classifier labels most account-related tickets 'Low', including several account-takeover reports that should be 'Urgent'. What is the MOST likely cause, and the BEST fix?

options.text: The examples are too similar, so Claude copied their pattern; replace them with a varied set covering different ticket types and every priority level.
The model is too small to tell security incidents apart from routine account requests; move the classifier to a more capable model and keep the examples.
The prompt lacks emphasis; add a capitalized instruction stating that account takeovers are ALWAYS urgent and must never be labelled Low under any circumstances.
Temperature is too high, which is making the labels drift between runs; set temperature to 0 so the classifier returns the same priority for similar tickets.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompting guidance says examples should be relevant and diverse, covering edge cases and varying enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns, and suggests 3 to 5 of them. Three nearly identical 'Low' examples teach 'account-related means Low'. A varied set across ticket types and priority levels removes the pattern.

whyWrong.B: The failures began when the examples were added, which points to the prompt. Nothing suggests the model cannot make the distinction.
whyWrong.C: Emphasis patches one symptom while leaving the misleading examples in place, and they will keep skewing other account-related tickets.
whyWrong.D: The labels are consistently wrong, not random. Lower temperature would make the biased answer more consistent, not more correct.

questions.mindset: Examples teach patterns, including ones you did not intend; make them diverse.

questions.stem: A due-diligence tool sends one request per question: first the analyst's question and instructions, then about 60,000 tokens of concatenated company filings. Answers often miss facts that are clearly stated deep in the filings, while questions about the first few pages are answered well. The team wants the cheapest fix to try first. What should the architect change?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window, so the filings take up a smaller share of the window and later pages get more attention.
Split the filings into chunks and send a separate request for each chunk, then ask Claude to merge the partial answers into one response for the analyst.
Repeat the question and instructions three times at intervals through the prompt so that Claude keeps them in mind while it reads through the filings.
Put the filings at the top of the prompt and the question and instructions at the end, and have Claude quote relevant passages before answering.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's long-context guidance says to place long documents near the top of the prompt, above the query and instructions (queries at the end improved quality by up to 30 percent in its tests, especially with complex multi-document inputs), and to have Claude quote the relevant parts first so it focuses on them. Both are prompt-layout changes with no extra cost, which suits a cheapest-first approach.

whyWrong.A: The input already fits. The problem is prompt structure, and a larger window does not change how the prompt is laid out.
whyWrong.B: Chunking multiplies requests and adds a merge step that can lose cross-document facts. It is more complex than a layout fix that should be tried first.
whyWrong.C: Repeating instructions adds tokens without addressing the recommended order of documents and query, and it is not a documented technique.

questions.mindset: For long inputs, documents first, question last, quotes before answers.

questions.scenario: A market-research firm produces client briefs through a four-step prompt chain: (1) extract claims from source articles, (2) deduplicate and cluster the claims, (3) draft the brief from the clusters, (4) polish tone and formatting. Since a recent change, 20% of final briefs omit important findings. Only the final brief is stored, and the eval grades only the final brief.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective way to find the cause?

options.text: Add an instruction to the polishing step to check the brief against the original articles and restore any missing findings before it is returned.
Log each step's output and evaluate the steps separately on the failing cases to find the first step where the important findings disappear.
Merge the four steps into one prompt so a single model call sees everything and can no longer drop information between steps.
Move all four steps to the most capable model available, since a stronger model is less likely to drop information at any step.

questions.explanation: A key benefit of chaining is that each step's output can be inspected and evaluated on its own. Here that benefit is being wasted because only the final output is stored. Logging intermediate outputs and checking where findings disappear (for example, clustering might be merging distinct claims) points the fix to the step that is actually failing.

whyWrong.A: That adds a self-check at the end to hide the symptom without finding where findings are lost. It also asks the polish step to do a job it was not designed for.
whyWrong.C: Merging the steps removes the visibility needed to debug and gives up the reasons the chain was built. It is a redesign made without a diagnosis.
whyWrong.D: Upgrading every step increases cost without knowing which step is at fault, and the cause may be a prompt or logic issue that a bigger model will not fix.

questions.mindset: In a pipeline, find the first step where the output goes wrong before fixing anything.

questions.stem: A procurement team extracts fields from supplier quotes into a JSON schema in which every field, including `discount_percent` and `warranty_months`, is required. Auditors find that when a quote states no discount or warranty, the output still contains plausible values such as 5 and 12. A validation retry loop is already in place and rarely triggers. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Add three few-shot examples of quotes that do contain a discount and warranty, so Claude learns where these fields usually appear.
Increase the number of validation retries, since a second or third attempt is more likely to notice that the values are not in the quote.
Make the fields nullable, and instruct Claude to return null when the quote does not state a value rather than estimating one.
Switch to a larger model, since a more capable model is less likely to fill fields with values that are not supported by the document.

questions.explanation: Requiring a value for information that may be absent pushes the model to invent one. Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends explicitly allowing Claude to say it does not know; in a schema, that means nullable fields plus an instruction to use null when the source does not say. The output is still valid JSON, so the validation retry loop never catches these values.

whyWrong.A: Examples that always include the fields reinforce the idea that a value should always be present. They do not show the correct behavior when it is absent.
whyWrong.B: The output is valid against the schema, so validation passes. More retries cannot create data that is not in the quote.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model may invent less often, but the schema still forbids the honest answer. The design flaw remains.

questions.mindset: If the schema has no place for 'not stated', the model will invent something to fill the slot.

questions.stem: A team migrated its research assistant to a newer Claude model and kept the same system prompt. The eval shows accuracy is unchanged, but the new model now does exactly what the prompt literally says. For example, with the instruction 'list the relevant papers' it returns a bare list, whereas the old model also added short summaries and suggested follow-up searches that users relied on. What should the architect conclude and do?

options.text: The new model is less capable at open-ended research tasks; roll back to the previous model and wait until a stronger generation is released.
The new model is truncating its output; raise max_tokens so there is room for the summaries and follow-up suggestions to be included again.
The new model needs a higher temperature to produce the extra content; raise it in steps until the summaries and suggestions come back.
The prompt relied on behavior the old model inferred; state the summaries and follow-up suggestions explicitly as requirements, then re-run the eval.

questions.explanation: Current Claude models are trained for precise instruction following. Anthropic's prompting guidance says that if you want 'above and beyond' behavior, you should ask for it explicitly rather than rely on the model inferring it. The prompt and model are mismatched, so the fix is to update the prompt and confirm with the eval, not to roll back the model.

whyWrong.A: Accuracy is unchanged, and the missing content was never requested. This is a prompt-to-model mismatch, not a capability drop.
whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests truncation (the lists are complete and would show a `max_tokens` stop reason if cut off). The model simply was not asked for more.
whyWrong.C: Temperature affects randomness, not whether the model does unrequested extra work. It would make output less predictable without reliably adding the content.

questions.mindset: After a model migration, re-read the prompt for behavior you never actually asked for.

questions.stem: A data-migration agent runs sessions of 150 or more tool calls, many of which return large query results. Early in a session it follows the user's constraints (for example 'never touch the archive schema'), but after about 100 calls it starts to repeat completed steps and occasionally violates a constraint. Errors are rare in short sessions. Which TWO changes MOST directly address the cause? Choose TWO.

options.text: Repeat the constraints in the system prompt with stronger wording, such as 'CRITICAL: NEVER touch the archive schema', so they are harder to overlook.
Move to a model with a larger context window so the whole session fits comfortably, which lets the agent see everything that has happened.
Clear or summarize old, bulky tool results once the agent has acted on them, keeping the context focused on what it still needs to finish the job.
Raise the temperature in long sessions so the agent explores new approaches instead of repeating steps it has already completed.
Have the agent keep a structured progress file of completed steps and active constraints outside the context, and re-read it as it works.

questions.explanation: The pattern (fine early, failing late, worse with bulky tool output) points to context degradation: as context fills with stale material, the model attends less reliably to what matters. Anthropic's context-engineering guidance recommends clearing or compacting old tool results and keeping structured notes outside the context window so key state and constraints are re-read rather than buried.

whyWrong.A: The constraint is already in the prompt, and it is followed early on. Louder wording does not solve the problem of it being buried under a growing context.
whyWrong.B: A bigger window holds more stale content but does not keep the model's attention on what matters. Recall degrades as context grows; curation, not capacity, is the fix.
whyWrong.D: Higher randomness does not restore lost state and makes constraint violations more likely, not less.

questions.mindset: Failures that appear only late in long sessions point to context, not capability: curate what stays in the window.

questions.stem: A compliance team asks an internal assistant to 'summarize the latest regulatory guidance on outsourcing and include links to the sources'. No documents are supplied and the assistant has no tools. Reviewers find that about a third of the links lead nowhere or to unrelated pages, though the summaries sound authoritative. Which TWO changes MOST directly address the problem? Choose TWO.

options.text: Give the assistant real sources, through a web search tool or retrieval over the regulator's publications, and have it answer only from what it actually retrieved.
Add an instruction that every link must be real and correct, and that the assistant should include only URLs it is certain exist and has seen before.
Use a larger model, since stronger models have memorized more regulatory sources and will therefore produce fewer incorrect or outdated links.
Before an answer is shown, programmatically fetch each cited URL and drop or flag any link that does not resolve or does not match the source it is said to be.
Ask the assistant to rate its confidence in each link from 1 to 10 and remove any link it rates below 7 before the answer is shown to reviewers.

questions.explanation: With no documents and no tools, the assistant can only produce links from memory, and 'latest' guidance may postdate its training data, so invented URLs are the expected failure. The fix has two parts. First, grounding: give it real sources (the web search tool returns results with cited source URLs; retrieval does the same for an internal corpus) and restrict it to them, which is what Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends. Second, a deterministic control: a link either resolves or it does not, so code, not the model, should verify every URL before reviewers see it.

whyWrong.B: Telling the model to be certain gives it nothing to check against. A model answering from memory cannot verify a URL, however firmly it is instructed to.
whyWrong.C: Any model answering from memory can produce links that look right but do not exist, and newer guidance may be more recent than its training data. Capacity is not the bottleneck.
whyWrong.E: Self-rated confidence is not reliable evidence that a link exists, and the check still has no source to verify against. Whether a URL resolves is a question for code, not for the model.

questions.mindset: You cannot prompt your way to real sources: give the model sources, then let code verify what it cites.
